content_html:
How often do Buddhas arise?

In Buddhist cosmology, the appearance of a Buddha is considered an exceptionally rare event. The frequency of Buddhas arising depends on the specific tradition and its understanding of time and cosmology. In some interpretations, millions or billions of years can pass between the appearance of one Buddha and the next.

The emergence of a Buddha depends on the accumulation of immense merit and wisdom through countless lifetimes. A Buddha arises in a world that has fallen into spiritual decline, where the Dhamma is no longer known and humanity is in need of guidance.

Theravāda Tradition

In Theravāda Buddhism, the time between Buddhas is described in terms of kalpas (eons), which are unimaginably long periods of time. A kalpa (eon) is divided into four stages: formation, existence, destruction, and void. It is during the existence phase that a Buddha might arise. A Buddha arises only when the teachings (Dhamma) of the previous Buddha have been forgotten, and the world is ready for a new teacher. Historical Buddhas include:

  • Kakusandha
  • Konāgamana
  • Kassapa
  • Gautama Buddha (the historical Buddha of our era)

The next Buddha will be Metteyya (Maitreya), predicted to arise in the distant future.

Mahāyāna Tradition

Mahāyāna Buddhism envisions a vast cosmos filled with countless Buddhas and bodhisattvas in different realms. Buddhas such as Amitābha and Vairocana are seen as eternal or active in other dimensions, making their “arising” less tied to linear time.

The Bodhisattva vow

The Bodhisattva vow is a central commitment in Mahāyāna Buddhism, taken by individuals who aspire to attain enlightenment not just for their own sake, but for the benefit of all sentient beings. By taking this vow, a person chooses to delay their own final liberation (nirvana) to remain in the cycle of birth and death (samsara) until all beings are free from suffering.

Core Components of the Bodhisattva Vow are:

  • Universal Compassion: The vow reflects the aspiration to help all beings without discrimination, embodying boundless compassion.
  • Altruistic Aspiration: The practitioner dedicates their efforts to achieving Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings.
  • Lifelong Commitment: The vow represents a lifelong (or even countless lifetimes-long) dedication to the path of a Bodhisattva.

The exact wording of the vow varies across traditions, but a common form is:

“Beings are numberless; I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible; I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless; I vow to enter them.
The Buddha way is unsurpassable; I vow to realize it.”

The vow marks the beginning of a spiritual journey that may take countless lifetimes. A Bodhisattva works tirelessly to alleviate the suffering of all beings while progressing toward enlightenment. It is both a deeply personal and universal undertaking, embodying the Mahāyāna ideal of selflessness and compassion.
